subsubtopic: OVERFISHING BY FOREIGN VESSELS-CALL FOR INCREASED AIR SURVEILLANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fishermen in our country depend on the fishery resources to survive. These resources have been threatened by the dramatic increase of infractions and overfishing by foreign offshore vessels. The number of violators caught and punished are just a drop in the bucket compared to the global problem. But what has the Government done to stop this illegal activity?
In a document released at the recent First Ministers' Conference, it was clearly pointed out that air surveillance and observer coverage were well below the effective levels established in the late 1970s. Air surveillance has been greatly reduced, by 550 air hours since 1970. Observer coverage on foreign vessels has been reduced by 50 per cent to 80 per cent.
Does the Government expect these violators to turn themselves in because they are overcome by remorse? If they are not caught, they cannot be prosecuted. The price of fish is high today. With a low likelihood of being apprehended, the risks are worth it. But these risks are taken at the price of Canadian fishermen. I demand that the Government increase its air surveillance and observer coverage on foreign vessels immediately, before there are no fish left for anyone to catch.

Mr. Speaker, very soon it will be a year since a now well-known project has been unveiled-the Matane paper mill. First I might indicate that, for some people, this project may have been oversimplified, even though Lower St. Lawrence and Gaspe residents view it as a rather challenging and extremely important venture.
Be that as it may, Mr. Speaker, given such protracted negotiations between the various interested parties, people
generally and my constituents in particular are now becoming increasingly concerned and wondering whether they are being taken for a ride.
Indeed no one would tax me with being excessive if I were to suggest that, in some respects, this project which has been bandied for over 20 years smacks of some kind of mental cruelty.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure you understand why my constituents now want the powers that be to honour their commitment and come up with an early decision on this matter which has .a serious impact on a region of our country where unemployment is rampant.

Mr. Speaker, a moratorium on the granting of fish farm licences is in effect in British Columbia while a Commission of Inquiry led by David Gillespie takes place. However, a real comprehensive study of the aquaculture industry is long overdue. The concerns of both aquaculturalists and traditional fishermen must be addressed. The fact that this Socred Commission has a mere two weeks to report, however, proves the present process a farce.
The federal Government has its own role to play in the granting of fish farm licences. It must ensure the environmental quality of salmon habitat and guard against the deposition of substances like tributyl tin and other chemicals that prove toxic to fish. British Columbians look to Ottawa for leadership but all they find is a Conservative administration which has not done one comprehensive public review of the budding aquaculture industry. Because of continued inaction, events have been allowed to proceed to the present state of chaos.

subtopic: S.O. 21 ABORTION CALL FOR MORE FREQUENT PUBLICATION OF STATISTICS
S.O. 21 ABORTION CALL FOR MORE FREQUENT PUBLICATION OF STATISTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was announced recently that Statistics Canada will only compile and publish complete socio-economic and medical data on abortions in Canada once every three years. In England and Wales information on legal abortion is not only published in regular annual reports, the agency concerned also publishes quarterly reports on abortions, including specific demographic and medical data.
Under the former Therapeutic Abortion Program of Statistics Canada, the interval between the date of data collection and the date of publication was about two years. We have no reason to believe this system will in any way be improved. Therefore, with complete data collected every three years, we can expect the next complete statistics to be compiled in 1988 and published in the year 1990.
The abortion issue is a vital one for all Canadians. We should be publishing this data more frequently, as is being done in Britain, not less frequently as Statistics Canada has recently announced.

subsubtopic: RURAL SERVICE-PRIVATIZATION OF LOCAL POST OFFICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a representative of a rural riding I am alarmed by what I see the federal Government doing to rural postal service in Canada in the name of cutting costs. Currently, Canada Post has 5,221 rural post offices. From the President's statement on November 20 it appears that there are 5,221 too many, not to mention rural route service. The plan is to turn 3,500 of these offices over to the private sector. One does not have to be a prophet to see the resulting variation of services in different areas with no national standards. The remaining 1,700 offices are to be amalgamated or replaced with multiple-site mailboxes.
When Canada Post was created it was established to extend its products and services and provide a standard of service that would meet the needs of the people of Canada. Neither these goals nor the rural way of life are obsolete but they could become so if the Government does not change its current tack.

Mr. Speaker, in most villages and smaller cities the post office is the only sign of a federal presence, the only place where residents can see the Canadian flag. The closure of rural post offices undermines Canadian unity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 7 I
spoke critically in the House of Canada's Ambassador to the United Nations, Mr. Stephen Lewis. Today I rise in praise of the Ambassador for his November 5 address to the United Nations in which he justifiably condemned U.S.S.R. Foreign Secretary Eduard Shevardnadze for his gross misrepresentation of events in Afghanistan as a "national democratic revolution". Mr. Lewis properly characterized this incredible description of Soviet intervention as a "linguistic mask designed to hide the brute face of oppression".
When Mr. Shevardnadze later complained that the UN debate on Afghanistan was destroying "the fruits" of the revolution, the Ambassador quickly cited the one million Afghan dead and asked "what revolutionary fruitfulness transforms an entire country into a killing field?" Canadians will not be appeased by pathetic rhetoric and Ambassador Lewis is to be commended for reminding the U.S.S.R. of that fact.

subtopic: PROPOSED SALE OF BANK OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
PROPOSED SALE OF BANK OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we will be seeking leave to introduce a special Bill this afternoon, something which I gather has been provided for by special agreement among all three Parties for consideration this afternoon.
Hon. Members have no doubt been aware for some time about media reports concerning the difficulties being faced by the Bank of British Columbia. Attention recently has been focused on the efforts of the bank to find a buyer to assume its assets and liabilities and to put the operation back on a strong financial footing. I am grateful to you, Mr. Speaker, and to
Members on all sides of the House for being able to bring this motion forward.
Recently, the search for a buyer intensified as the financial condition of the bank continued to weaken as a result of the erosion of its capital base. This erosion was caused by nonperforming loans. For the past several weeks, at the request of the bank, the federal and British Columbia Governments have been assisting in the effort to find a buyer to carry on the business of the bank. This effort has been successful. I am speaking today because the bank has requested the assistance of the House now in facilitating the sale of its operations. Our role is to facilitate this sale.
In responding to this request the Government has been guided by four basic considerations. First, such a transaction should ensure the long-term financial viability of the ongoing institution.

Second, such a transaction should provide to the fullest extent possible for the needs of the depositors, other creditors, borrowers and shareholders.

Further, and this is most important, it should result in a strong regionally-based institution to serve the needs of the western-most part of our country. Finally, this should be done without the expenditure of federal public funds as part of the purchase agreement. In short, the buyer of the bank should be able to inject new capital, maintain the confidence of depositors, assume its assets and liabilities and keep the bank operating as a going concern.
During the search for a buyer a few institutions indicated some degree of interest in the Bank of British Columbia. However, in the opinion of the management and the board of the bank, only one proposal adequately meets the needs of depositors, other creditors, borrowers and shareholders. It has been put forward by the Hongkong Bank of Canada, a subsidiary of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation. The board of directors of the Bank of British Columbia met in special session to give its formal approval to the offer and to request that the Government propose legislation to Parliament to facilitate the sale.
The Government has determined that this purchase fully meets the basic considerations that I have outlined, the four objectives to which I have spoken. The purchaser is a subsidiary of one of the world's largest banks. It has the resources to maintain and strengthen the business of the Bank of British Columbia, and it has pledged to do so. In fact, it will be obligated to do so if we agree to this transaction. Moreover, the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation is firmly based in the Pacific Rim, as is the Bank of British Columbia. As many Hon. Members are aware, Premier Vander Zalm has publicly indicated his preference for a Pacific Rim bank. Furthermore, he has endorsed this transaction with enthusiasm, as has the Government.
November 26, 1986

The management of the Bank of British Columbia has advised the Government that this transaction is necessary for its survival, and the Government agrees with that assessment. The rapidly worsening condition of the bank has been closely monitored by the Office of the Inspector General of Banks.
I would like to quote from the press release issued by the Bank of British Columbia just a few moments ago which contains the details of the transaction. It states:
The board of directors of the Bank of British Columbia believes that it is essential for BBC to enter into a transaction if liquidation is to be avoided and further believes that no other transaction can be identified that would be as beneficial as the proposed transaction with Hongkong Bank of Canada.

Liquidation would not be in the interests of the Bank's 1900 employees, its depositors, other creditors, borrowers and shareholders. It would not be in the interests of the Province of British Columbia and it would not be in the interests of the Canadian banking system.

As part of the initiative to ensure that the business of the bank continues, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation has agreed to extend the sum of $200 million to help recapitalize the bank. I remind Hon. Members that the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation is funded entirely from premiums paid by deposit-taking institutions. There will be no impact on the Government's deficit.
The only realistic alternative, as the bank's board has indicated, would be for the bank to shut its doors. The cost of paying the insured depositors in this situation would be considerably greater than $200 million. Consistent with its statutory authority, the board of directors of CDIC has determined that this payment will minimize future losses for the corporation. The board of the CDIC must determine in matters of this sort whether it will pay less than it ordinarily would through liquidation unless it is determined very clearly.
I would like to explain briefly the role the House is being asked to play in facilitating this transaction. Ordinarily we would say that this is a transaction which has been done, why are we taking the time of the House in this matter? Sections 273 to 275 of the Bank Act provide that the sale of bank assets and liabilities be approved at a shareholders' meeting 28 days after formal notice is given of the terms of sale. What has happened is that the Government has been requested by the board of directors of the Bank of British Columbia to avoid the uncertainty that would be created by such a delay and thereby to minimize disruption for depositors and borrowers. Accordingly, Parliament is being asked to enact the necessary legislation to enable the transaction to be completed on a timely basis.
The legislation recognizes the interests of shareholders. It provides for a shareholders' meeting with 14 days' notice to approve the consideration received for the sale of the bank's assets. Or, if shareholders so choose, when they have their meeting they can choose to have an independent assessor
Statements by Ministers
appointed to evaluate the value of their shares immediately prior to the time of sale. This evaluation by the assessor would be binding.
This Bill facilitates a solution that is in the interests of depositors and other creditors, borrowers and shareholders of the Bank of British Columbia. It is in the interests of the Province of British Columbia and very much in the interests of the Canadian banking system.

I ask Hon. Members to adopt this Bill immediately.

I urge immediate and unanimous approval. This piece of legislation will ensure the safety we need for the depositors, other creditors, borrowers, employees and branches of that bank in the province. It will also ensure a window to the Pacific Rim, to the connections and network of the Pacific Rim that the financial system of British Columbia has long wanted. I am very pleased to bring this Bill before the House and I thank Hon. Members on all sides for making this possible.

Before that, those of us representing constituencies in British Columbia had some understanding of the difficulty in which the Bank found itself. This action shows how badly the Government has managed the rebuilding of confidence in our financial institutions. We have been waiting for two years for the proposed reform package for financial institutions. We still do not have it. The Canadian public is still waiting. Of course, another stop-gap, ad hoc measure is being taken to rescue a bank at the last moment.
Taking you back a bit in history, Mr. Speaker, the Bank of British Columbia was at the leading edge of the aspirations of the people of the province and western Canada to have their own financial institutions. They wanted to do things their own way at their own speed and to have credit authorizations given by British Columbians who lived in the province close to where the people seeking credit lived. It was created in part at the behest of the late W. A. C. Bennett, then Premier of the Province of British Columbia. Despite political differences, he was certainly one of the great institution builders of British Columbia.
I recall that Premier Bennett came personally to Ottawa in 1967 to ask the Government to incorporate the Bank of British

November 26, 1986
Statements by Ministers
Columbia. He sat in the Prime Minister's gallery while the Bill was being debated. He personally attended the opening of the first branch of the Bank and he summoned all British Columbians to give it their full support.
The Bank of British Columbia has played an important role in bringing about the creation of small and medium-sized businesses in British Columbia and, indeed, throughout western Canada. It proved that in British Columbia the best decisions for small and medium-sized businesses were made closer to the businesses and operations concerned. That is why the regional banking system was so welcomed in western Canada.
At the beginning of 1985 the Bank of British Columbia was the most conservatively financed financial institution of its size in the country. It had a leverage ratio about comparable to the average ratio of the leading banks in Canada. It had very little foreign exposure and, of course, it had a substantial market share in British Columbia. Many of the problems it is having today originated with the collapse of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank.
You know our views on the collapse of those two banks, Mr. Speaker. The banks were very badly mismanaged to begin with but the way the Government handled that crisis led to the current instability in the banking system and later effected the forced merger of the Continental Bank with Lloyd's of London and now the proposed arrangement between the Hongkong Bank and the Bank of British Columbia.
The Government made two grave errors. When the Minister of Finance and the predecessor of the Minister of State for Finance brought the bail-out package to Parliament, we asked the Ministers and indeed the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) whether or not the bail-out package was sufficient. We were assured that it was, but it turned out that the Ministers and officials had not bothered to look at the books of the Canadian Commercial Bank. The arrangement was insufficient. On the basis of what the Minister of Finance, the Governor of the Bank and the Minister of State for Finance's predecessor said, people continued to deposit money in those banks as well as in the Continental Bank and the Bank of British Columbia.
A year ago September, it was found that the package was indeed inadequate and the Government had misrepresented the viability and solvency of those two banks to Parliament and the Canadian people. As a result of that lack of confidence, both the Continental Bank and the Bank of British Columbia have had repeated difficulties in persuading other banks, large corporations and credit unions to maintain deposits. I can understand that. The teasurer of a major organization, a town council or a municipality has a fiduciary role to play. He must protect the money of his shareholders or taxpayers. Therefore, both banks, the Continental Bank and the Bank of British Columbia, had a difficult time persuading other banks and depositors to stay with them.
We blamed the Government on these two issues. First it did not know what it was doing when it brought in the original
bail-out package for the Canadian Commercial Bank. Second, it misrepresented the facts to the Canadian people and Parliament between March and September. Mr. Justice Estey confirmed that the bail-out was an amateur night effort and that it was insufficient. He confirmed as well that the two banks had not been solvent.
We are now being asked to provide a hurried solution in the form of a sale of assets of the Bank of British Columbia to the Hongkong Bank of Canada, a Schedule B bank. The parent bank is one of the world's largest and best managed banks. The headquarters of the subsidiary of the Bank is in Vancouver and thus we understand that the executive direction of the Bank of B.C. division of the new bank will be maintained in Vancouver. This provides at least some solace for the regional aspirations of British Columbians. There will at least be one institution of its size with a head office in British Columbia.
The employees of the Bank of British Columbia, some 1,400 in number, will, I am advised, have continuing employment assured, and I hope the Minister will assure us of this during the course of the debate. I am also told that the 39 branches of the Bank will continue to be open for the time being. The Bill will obviously be of some assistance to the employees and will assure some 200,000 depositors of the safety of their funds.
I am not unmindful of the fact that the CDIC, an agent of the Government of Canada, is declaring a loss of some $200 million in connection with the Bank of B.C. It is our understanding from what the Minister of State for Finance has told us that if this Bill is not passed today or tomorrow the shareholders themselves stand to lose whatever net worth is today available to them. Frankly, although we want to hear more about it during the course of debate, this is probably the only reason that I personally would agree to a Bill of this kind.
The Bill limits drastically and in a Draconian fashion the rights of shareholders under the Bank Act. The Hon. Minister is frowning, but he knows about the delays that are necessarily incurred in sending out notices telling shareholders that they have the right to approve of or disagree with any merger or deal like this. From what I understand the Minister to say, under this Bill the shareholders will be limited to either approving or disapproving of the amount of the deal, not the deal itself. That is a very drastic limitation of the rights of shareholders, and we will require proof here in the House that that is necessary.

Before the Bill is adopted by the House, Mr. Speaker, I think we should insist that the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs be ?'lowed to proceed with a full review, as it did in the case of the Continental Bank and Lloyds, review, with witnesses and officers of the two banks appearing before the Committee, so that we as Members of this House will have the assurance that there was indeed an emergency and a pressing need to have this Bill adopted.
November 26, 1986

It is deplorable that the Government should only this morning spring a request for parliamentary action in these circumstances. It is not a compliment to Parliament.

It is without a doubt an admission of incompetence on the part of the Government and it is one more example of the state of complete disarray of the Government's policies, especially where the banks are concerned, and as I said at the beginning of my speech, it reflects the utter chaos caused by the Government originally in the case of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northlands Bank several months ago in this House.

However, I believe in the interests of British Columbians as depositors, employees, and shareholders, that we are compelled to accept the Government's representation. As to the need for haste, we are going to hold the Government responsible in demonstrating to us and to the country the need for that urgency, the need for a restricted debate, the need for the restriction on the right of the shareholders of the bank. We will want that confirmed in a hearing of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs after this debate is concluded.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we come to this issue understanding the urgency-if the representations of the Government can be accepted at face value-but still stung by the experience that we had in this House in March, 1985 when the Minister of Finance and the then Minister of State for Finance brought us a bail-out package for the Canadian Commercial Bank. We were misled. The Government did not know what it was doing. It had not searched the books. Parliament was taken for a ride. We do not underestimate the gravity of the situation. We do not underestimate what the Minister of Finance told me personally, and what the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) told Parliament this afternoon. The burden of proof is clearly on the Government. We are relying on the Government.

subtopic: PROPOSED SALE OF BANK OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this particular project is brought forward because of the situation of the Bank of British Columbia. It is a regional bank. Members of my Party, and particularly my colleagues who come from western Canada, are very much concerned about the continuing need for regional banking in western Canada. Whether that will be achieved with this particular proposed takeover by the Hongkong Bank is another matter. Within the time that is available, which is not long, and for reasons that I will come to shortly, essentially on this side of the House we are not in a position to judge whether or not the Government has taken the correct course of action.
I have some substantial misgivings over what the Government is prepared to do. However, having only been brought
Statements by Ministers
into the Government's confidence on this issue at 9.15 this morning, our role is simply to decide whether to adopt this measure in the course of the next day or two, or to string it out and let it take a week or two weeks, whichever it might take, if the parliamentary devices available to us were used, or if the matter was to be referred to the Commons finance committee for a hearing prior to passage some time early next week.
It has been represented to me and to my Party that delay at this time would or could lead to difficulties for the Bank of British Columbia in terms of its deposit base, and that that in turn would affect the viability of the bank in terms of its ability to do business in British Columbia and Alberta under the new ownership. I accept that that argument has some validity. Therefore, since the only solution that the Government has been prepared to put forward has been this particular takeover, we are in the position of either saying that we are going to resist it, although we are not in a position to put forward an alternative because we do not have the facts or the number of seats in the House to make that work, or alternatively to simply accept the Government's decision.
Let us be very clear that this is a Government decision. The only role that Parliament can play is to decide whether we wish to make this decision and allow this decision to become law by tomorrow evening, or to string this out for another few days. I have had occasion to speak to people in financial circles in Vancouver, including people from the Vancouver City Savings Credit Union, which was in very serious discussions with the Bank of British Columbia a few days ago. It is disappointed at being excluded from doing a deal with the Bank of British Columbia, largely because of a policy decision by this Government. It, too, indicates that if it is going to be done at all, it is better to do it in a couple of days than to allow the agony to continue.
Let us be very clear that the Government says in the statement of the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) that it is important to retain a strong and regionally based institution to serve the needs of the most western part of Canada. It is questionable whether that will be what is achieved by this particular measure.
I do know that the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, using what are essentially public funds, will advance $200 million to the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank, the parent company of the Hongkong Bank of Canada. The parent Hongkong Bank will then turn around and give $60 million to the subsidiary, and that in turn will be passed on to the Bank of British Columbia in return for transferring substantially all of its assets and liabilities.
In other words, we Canadians, if I can be simple about it, are paying $200 million to a foreign institution so that they can take over the control of a $3 billion Canadian bank. That is essentially what the Government is telling us is the best solution that was available for this important regional institution in British Columbia, an institution which was founded with high hopes some 10 years ago, and which has

November 26, 1986
Business of the House
extended service to many people in western Canada over the course of the last couple of years.
The Government is also telling us that the asset base of the Bank of British Columbia was sound, according to the Inspector General of Banks and a special team review, in October, 1985. At that time the bank portfolio was studied in detail. The Inspector General told us that it was okay, in fact that loan loss experience was going down. The Government is now telling us that there is an over-all erosion of those assets which, by my calculation, is somewhere in the nature of $300 million to $350 million. This is enough to wipe out the equity of both the preferred and the ordinary shareholders of the bank, and then to contribute to a loss of some $150 million, or thereabouts.
Nonetheless, the Government is stating that in its wisdom and opinion the shareholders and the preferred shareholders of the Bank of British Columbia should be repaid to the extent- not a lot, I agree-of $60 million or $75 million. That money essentially is going to come from the taxpayers, at least for the next six or seven years.
The Minister's statement is that this payment to the Hongkong Bank, so it can take over our Canadian bank, is being made without the expenditure of federal public funds as part of the purchase arrangements. I have had occasion to look at the annual report of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. At the end of 1985 this institution was in the hole to the extent of $1.25 billion. It was paying that off at the rate of about $200 million a year through an increase in premiums, which went through the House a few months ago. The $200 million which is now being advanced from the Consolidated Revenue Fund, that is, from the taxpayers to CDIC to go to the Hongkong Bank, will not, therefore, be repaid until 1993, assuming that the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation has no further losses to contend with-no other institutions go bust or require its assistance over the course of the next six or seven years.
I recognize that the situation is difficult. Financial markets are changing very rapidly. But I wish to point out that the Government could have had a regional solution with control in the head office fully under the control of British Columbians by means of assistance to the Vancouver City Savings Credit Union proposal. Apparently the Government of British Columbia was not prepared to go along with that particular measure, and neither was the federal Government. The Government could have kept control of the Bank of British Columbia's business in Canada, because there are at least a couple of Schedule A banks, the Bank of Nova Scotia and the Toronto-Dominion Bank, which are not heavily represented in their branch network in western Canada, and from which there would have been a good fit if discussions on a merger or takeover of assets had been encouraged by the Government, rather than discouraged or ignored. Instead, the Government has chosen a foreign solution which will cost everyone who gets bank interest over the course of the next year or so $1 for every
$1,000 of investment. If I may put it in very practical terms, that will be the cost.
I hope we will receive a commitment from the Government that the matter will go before the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs after the Bill has receivd passage tomorrow. For the reasons I have given, we have agreed, although we have questions about the Bill, that it should at least come to a conclusion tomorrow. However, I believe that the issue should not be forgotten because the Bill itself goes to third reading and is then given approval by the Senate and Royal Assent.
This is ad hoc banking policy. The Government has had two years to implement a policy on financial institutions. It has not done so. Canadians are now paying the price. They are paying the price in terms of the $1 billion or so we advanced in respect of the failure of two western banks the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. Now they are paying an additional price. One way or another, as taxpayers, depositors, or customers of Canadian banks, every Canadian will participate in the cost of $200 million which is now being advanced to take control of the Bank of British Columbia. It will take control out of British Columbia hands, out of regional hands, out of Canadian hands, and put it into the hands of the Hongkong Bank.

CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE Mrs. Shirley Martin (Lincoln) moved:
Motions
That the first report of the Special Committee on Child Care, presented to the House on Wednesday, November 19, be concurred in.
She said: Mr. Speaker, in requesting concurrence in the report of the Special Committee on Child Care, I am asking the House for the opportunity to table a quality document reflecting the evidenced needs of Canadian children and parents, while making responsible suggestions for government action through the range of components which comprise the child care delivery system in Canada.
Our committee travelled to every province and territory in Canada to listen to the needs and recommendations of Canadians. The response was impressive. Over 2,000 people were heard and almost 900 written submissions were received. In addition, existing research in the field required investigation, and new research was required. As we reviewed our initial report, we determined that to rush the preparation of this document would be a great disservice to the people of Canada.
I know that Hon. Members of both opposition Parties join with me in their concerns that the report provide the best available research and recommendations. Therefore, in the interest of all Canadians, especially the children of Canada, I respectfully ask that this extension be granted with the approval of all Hon. Members of the House.

Mr. Speaker, unfortunately, I cannot accept a proposal by the Chairman of the Special Committee on Child Care for an extension for the Committee's report. In fact I find it very distressing. When we consider the urgent need for daycare centres, asking for an extension of several months does seem rather strange. I might have been agreeable to an extension of several weeks, but I think that in the circumstances, several months is out of the question.
All we have to do is go back to the reports of the various commissions of inquiry, including the Bird Commission and the Report on Equality in Employment, where the situation is described and identified as a priority, because something must be done for children, not just for children from zero to five but also for children from six to fourteen, especially when we consider that 54 per cent of our children are alone after school.
We have had a parliamentary committee that travelled across the country and heard a number of briefs, many from parents who were unanimous in urging the Government to take action and do so very soon.
I read news reports on the First Ministers' Conference last week, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said quite clearly that it was very important for women to have employment equity and that he felt employment equity started with
1550

November 26, 1986
Motions
daycare. I would like to remind him-of course daycare centres are important for women-but he said that daycare was a women's problem, and I would like to say here to the Prime Minister that daycare is a problem for society and for our families, not just for women.
He also said that he intended to start consultations with the provincial governments. I am all in favour of consultations with the provincial governments, but since 1984 when the Conservative Government and this Prime Minister came to power, all we have seen has been consultations and discussions. I think that it is important for the Government to act and to stop consulting because this is a priority issue. Each child is entitled to daycare services.
It is rather shocking to see that the only result we have had is still more consultation. It is difficult to believe that the Prime Minister really wants to take action.
Our Committee voted to request an emergency fund of $150 million in the next Budget in January 1987, because the Prime Minister has said several times since his Government has been in power that the 1987 Budget would provide the allocations needed for child care programs. The report would by then have been tabled in the House. The Prime Minister also said in Vancouver that the funds would be allocated. If the Conservative Government is really serious about child care, it will allocate at least $ 150 million as an emergency fund to be used from February 1987 until the report of the Parliamentary Commission is implemented, perhaps one year from now.
In addition, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has asked for a Social Affairs Ministers' Conference in January 1987. If the Government wants to show its commitment to child care, one of the priorities at this conference should be to examine this issue because the only way we can know whether the Government wants to give priority to child care services will be to see it do it with our own eyes.
We have been hearing about daycare centres for two years, but this should not remain at the level of lip service or be simply an exercise in public relations. If the Government is truly serious, the first thing to do is to prepare the report quickly and the second is to make sure that the amounts allocated in the next budget are large enough to provide an emergency fund as well as daycare services for our children. Moreover, the Minister of National Health and Welfare should make this a priority issue at this meeting next January.

Mr. Speaker, there is no question at all that adequate funding of quality child care services is one of the most important issues facing the Government, and especially the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).
I am very concerned that the report of the Special Committee on Child Care will be delayed to March 21, long after the 1987 budget has been prepared and presented. We would have
preferred to have extended the reporting date to January 21 so as to include recommendations for funding in the upcoming budget. This delay leaves one to suspect that despite the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) lip service again last week in Vancouver, the federal Government does not intend to introduce federal initiatives to deal with the well-documented child care emergency in the coming year. Obviously the Government prefers to delay such action until just before the next election when the Government can say: "Look what we are doing for children and families". The Government wants to leave it to provincial Governments to initiate action in the child care field knowing that this will be delayed for several years.
We opposed this motion in committee, Mr. Speaker. We do not approve of a delay unless Government Members are prepared to support a motion which I presented to the committee for emergency federal funding for child care services. The motion I presented last week reads:
That the committee request the Minister of Finance to include in the upcoming budget a child care fund of up to $150 million to be used as an emergency fund for stabilizing and upgrading child care services until the committee report is tabled and implemented.
This is a very reasonable request. I hate to use the word, but it is a very conservative request. As a matter of fact, the New Democratic Party for several years has advocated federal expenditures in direct grants of up to $320 million. We estimate that this amount is needed to upgrade the quality of existing day care services to help reduce fees so that that care is affordable, and to create an additional 25,000 new child care spaces. This money would also cover a development fund to assist poorer regions and native communities which have a deplorable lack of child care services.
I expect a positive answer to the motion I presented, which I am glad to say was seconded by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) of the Official Opposition. As a result of the presentation, several questions have been raised in relation to the request. First, is there a child care emergency? Second, funding should be based on sound research and planning.
Speaking quickly to the emergency, there is no question that there is a national case of child neglect in Canada. This was documented extensively in the Chile Care Committee report and has been repeated over and over again in public hearings held across Canada. The lives and well being of children are at risk in an informal babysitting arrangement because working parents simply have no other alternative. There is no licenced monitored child care in many communities, and if there is, most parents cannot afford it.
One working mother told us she had to use nine different babysitters in the first year of her child's life. She had to work because her family was living on poverty income. Many children have no care at all or are left in the care of older siblings.
We were told repeatedly of concerns about latch-key children who go home to an empty house and who have
November 26, 1986

unsupervised situations during the summer months because there is no affordable child care.
Many day care centres have questionable standards. Children are being placed in situations where care is not up to the standard it should be. Centres are forced to charge fees that are too high. They pay very low wages to care givers because child care centres are grossly underfunded.
The only way centres can improve their standard of care is with direct government grants to help defray overhead costs, to reduce fees and to pay adequate wages. Dedicated care givers will continue to subsidize child care across the country. Many of these people are burning out and leaving the field because the federal Government refuses to act in this year's budget. Many long hours at minimum wages are expected of care givers. This refutes the statements made by the Prime Minister in Vancouver about equality. The Government is condoning the exploitation of women workers by refusing adequate funding for child care services in the upcoming year.
Many communities have no licensed child care services at all. Children of farm families are left alone in unsafe conditions. There are no services for children in northern and isolated communities and native communities. Shift workers and seasonal workers need flexible hour care. They have none. Children are often removed from their homes in native communities because there is no emergency care and no support of family services. This is a tragedy.
Funding should be based on a sound plan, of course. I agree, Mr. Speaker. A team of researchers and experts spent several years documenting the needs resulting in the Cooke report. They came up with an adequate plan advocating good faith grants from the federal Government that would stabilize existing services and establish a floor of good quality services until provinces can develop a comprehensive, affordable system of quality child care right across Canada. The Cooke report also proposed that federal grants be available as conditional grants to every province and territory on condition that funds be forwarded to licensed non-profit centres to provide operating and capital funds until cost sharing arrangements can be worked out with the provinces.
The Cooke report also proposed a formula. The plans are there. The research is there, Mr. Speaker. All we need is the Government will to start in 1987 with some up-front funding to show its intentions are right. We are tired of platitudes and words from the Prime Minister and others which really mean nothing unless there are some funds available to do something about this drastic emergency.
I am surprised that the Minister responsible for the Status of women yesterday in committee would say to me: "If it was just a matter of direct grants, Margaret, your committee would come out with a one-line report." That shows how little that Minister knows about the situation. There have been 15 years of reports that documented the needs. Obviously the Minister has not studied the Cooke report which provides an
Motions
adequate funding mechanism and formula that could be adopted in the upcoming budget.
I repeat to this House and the Government that the need for adequate funding of child care services is urgent. Children are being damaged, dedicated care givers are being exploited and working parents are being subjected to unnecessary stress and worry while the Government apparently is refusing to take action in providing any funds in this year's budget.
The Prime Minister's promises last week are a laugh. He talked about equality. Obviously he wants the women's vote. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, he is not going to get it unless he puts some money where his mouth is. We are appalled at his lack of understanding. The main need in the whole field of child care is for some out front federal funding and it must be in this year's budget. That is why we do not want to delay any longer. We want to go forward with a proposal for emergency funding in this year's budget and we want to get our committee report out just as quickly as possible.
Motion agreed to.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I will be brief. I just want to make a few comments in reply to some of the questions posed a few minutes ago.
First, the urgency of this legislation has been explained. I agree with the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) who identified precisely what this Bill will do. It does not prevent shareholders from meeting to determine compensation. It will allow that to happen. He understood that clearly. The Bill also deals with winding up and so on which I can explain when it goes to committee.
The issue of financial institution reform has been a major priority of this Government. It has been decades since we have had financial institution reform. We propose to bring forward a comprehensive set of reforms very shortly. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition expressed his concern that we would be making ad hoc decisions forever unless this reform takes place. The new framework will be put in place very shortly, but
November 26, 1986

until then, of course, we operate within the existing framework. It is my hope we can bring it in very shortly and that it will cover essentially both parts of the financial institution regime, that being inspection and supervision. It will address all of the problems that Mr. Justice Estey referred to which concern Canadians regarding the liability of inspection and supervision of deposit-taking institutions, insurance and trust companies. Nothing has been done in this regard for literally decades and I am very proud to have the opportunity to bring in major changes which will further strengthen the Canadian financial system. I will not speak further about that because the time will come for that.
The second part of our task over the next few months is to come to terms with the rules of the game, so to speak, as they affect ownership and the function of financial institutions. As we all know, financial institutions would like to broaden their base of activity. What should be the parameters? Who should be able to own a financial institution? How big should they be? Those questions have been examined in very great detail through a host of studies, foremost of which would be in the standing committee of this House. That committee had important things to say on these subjects. As well, the Senate dealt with it, and there have been important studies at the provincial level. Then we have the Estey report. 1 would say that never has a subject been better researched or prepared for than financial institution reform. Therefore we are ready for reform and ready to bring in the package. I will be consulting with provincial Ministers on this issue on Sunday and Monday. That is one of the very last steps we must take in order to bring the package forward. I hope all Members will agree that this package will greatly strengthen the system and lay down rules so that business plans can be made and the activities of our financial sector can grow and prosper. I believe depositors will feel more secure and borrowers will find a more competitive environment. We will be internationally competitive, rather than a financial non-competitive island unto ourselves. This massive new structure will be in place shortly.
In my view, the Bill before us is a symbol of the confidence that foreign banking institutions show toward this country. Our banking system must be extremely strong to attract this kind of interest. While I share with my colleagues a concern about too much foreign ownership, the transaction we are being asked to facilitate today constitutes only approximately 1 per cent of the Canadian banking system. I believe that Schedule B banks will move from 10.7 per cent to 11.8 per cent of the total assets of the Canadian banking system, so that this is not a massive foreign invasion of the Canadian banking system.
When the Bank Act was changed in 1980, we explicitly wanted to have foreign institutions admitted to Canada. This would allow reciprocal rights for our financial institutions abroad because they cannot operate effectively unless there is an opportunity for foreign institutions here. Second, we wanted
Bank of British Columbia Business Continuation Act
the competition and the skills that foreign entry can sometimes bring. What better example of that than this legislation?
In my opinion, this legislation is the quintessential example of the importance of having Schedule B banks at certain times because it allows the skills, contacts and the network that exists in the Pacific Rim with one of the largest banks in the world to be linked with the Bank of British Columbia.
Let me make it clear that banks that are constituted as Schedule B banks are not branches. They are separate corporations with their own directors and a Canadian head office. It is important to note that it is a Canadian operation. The Bank of British Columbia will have its head office here and the majority of directors will be Canadian. Its branches and employees will remain in place. By giving it this transfusion, I believe we have found a way not only to save an institution that was wounded, perhaps fatally, it will be stronger and more robust than ever. That is the purpose of the Bill.
Furthermore, this legislation will add a presence in the Pacific Rim that British Columbia has never had. I know that Hon. Members will want to deal with the importance of this to Canada and the western part of our country. This Bill represents an act of confidence and makes proper use of the provisions of the Bank Act.
Let me deal with how the operations of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation are affected by this transaction. The CDIC is an institution with its own board, and operates on premiums it receives from member institutions. Its decision on whether to make a transfusion of $200 million is based on the consideration of whether it will ultimately pay less through this transfusion than if the Bank of British Columbia were liquidated. That is the decision that the CDIC is making, and it has been constituted to make those kinds of judgments.
There is concern that we are asked to make last minute decisions. Decisions on any transactions such as this often must be made quickly. Quite frankly, this is an opportunity for the CDIC to minimize its obligations while allowing the bank to grow and prosper.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in the Official Opposition have agreed with some reluctance to the Government's request to consider and pass this legislation immediately. Our reluctance was overcome by our wish to safeguard the jobs involved and to avoid disrupting the regional economy. However, we take strong exception to the habit the Government has developed of ad hoc regulation and legislation in the financial services industry. It is ad hoc because, despite the promises in two Throne Speeches, we have had no reform legislation on financial institutions. The Government continues to operate in a policy vacuum.
All of us remember only too well when, on March 25, 1985, the former Minister of State for Finance announced the Government's decision to bail out the Canadian Commercial Bank and asked for the co-operation of the House in passing the enabling legislation immediately. We agreed and found out later that the information we were given was totally inaccurate. The Government gave guarantees that with the bail-out package the Canadian Commercial Bank could be viable. We found later that those guarantees were worthless. The Government did not know and did not use information which was available.
When the committee on finance examined the situation, after the passage of the legislation, it became clear that the loan assets of the Canadian Commercial Bank had not been accurately valued and that there were many problems with its administration. These were problems of which the Government should have been aware but was not. There was a Memorandum of Understanding signed but there was a 30-day period before that memorandum was confirmed. In that 30-day period, the Government made no serious examination of the loan assets, even though the other banks participating in the bail-out had requested this be done.
Therefore, we in the official Opposition agreed to give passage to a Bill in the spring of 1985 because we believed the Government. We accepted the undertakings we were given, but later we found these undertakings were worth nothing.
Even up to mid-August of 1985, the Government was still saying that with the bail-out package it had arranged, the Canadian Commercial Bank was viable. Yet, as we know, by September 1 it was in liquidation.
Perhaps we should be appreciative of the fact that the Government is not seeking that sort of arrangement this time. However, we would not be responsible members of the Opposition if we did not insist on better information from the Government than we were given a year and a half ago. We intend to hold the Government responsible for the accuracy of information it brings forward in this debate. Our passing of this Bill is conditional on our receiving an assurance that the matter will receive a very thorough examination afterward by the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs.
After the bail-out of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank depositors last year, there was the takeover of Canada Trust, a financial institution, the fourth largest holder of personal savings accounts in Canada, by the industrial giant, Imasco Limited. This was a clear situation of a financial institution coming under the control of a nonfinancial group, which is something the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs had recommended against in its report on the Government's Green Paper on the Regulation of Financial Institutions. However, the Government has not responded to that report, nor indeed has it responded to any of the stack of reports on financial deregulation. Therefore, when the Canada Trust-Imasco deal came up, the Government had no legislation in place to deal with it, with the less than satisfactory result that the deal was approved but the new owner was asked to give certain undertakings. Again, we have an ad hoc solution.
On October 2 this year, there was the announcement that the Government had approved a sale of assets enabling the British owned Lloyd's Bank to take over the Continental Bank which is, or was, a Canadian bank. Again, we in the official Opposition directed our criticism not at the particular transaction but at the Government, because yet again it had put itself in the position of having to make important and
November 26, 1986

precedent setting decisions involving financial institutions without the benefit of a policy framework. That is no way to govern.
As I have said before on a number of occasions in this Elouse, the process of reform of financial institutions' legislation began with the previous Government and bogged down with the present Government at a time when the need for it is becoming clearer and clearer. The pace of change in the financial services industry is not slackening, it is accelerating. The Government must get a handle on this to ensure that these changes work in the best interests of Canadians.
Almost a year and a half ago the Government made a hasty and ill-considered decision to bail out a bank. Less than six months later that bank and another small regional bank had failed amid well founded charges of Government mismanagement and misinformation. Since then it has become more and more obvious that the Government has failed in its responsibility to restore stability and confidence to the banking industry, and that small Canadian regional banks have been the major casualties.
Look at the evidence, Mr. Speaker. First, the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank failed and are now in liquidation. Then the dominos began to topple. Morguard Bank was taken over by Security Pacific Bank of Canada, a subsidiary of a U.S. based parent. The Mercantile Bank was taken over by the Canadian owned National Bank, or Banque national. Last month the Continental Bank was taken over by British-owned Lloyds Bank. Now we have the Bank of British Columbia going in with the Hongkong Bank. What is happening to the regional banks under this Government? It seems that they are disappearing one by one in the fall-out from that ill-fated attempt to save the Canadian Commercial Bank, a bank which, as Mr. Justice Estey has confirmed, was already dead on its feet.
The Bank of British Columbia, on the other hand, was by all accounts a healthy institution before the CCB bail-out raised fears and anxieties which spread to all small regional banks and financial institutions. As my leader said earlier, in January 1985 the leverage ratio of the Bank of British Columbia stood at 13 as compared to an industry average of over 20. It was in sound condition but, faced with the Government's poor handling of affairs at the Canadian Commercial Bank, it just could not recover the investor and depositor confidence on which financial institutions depend for their life and health.
The press release issued today by the Bank of British Columbia does indeed point the finger fairly clearly at the relationship between that bank's difficulties and the Government's actions in relation to the Canadian Commercial Bank. There is a reference in the news release to the fact that the Bank of British Columbia has been canvassing for possible partners or successors with the ability to carry on the business of the Bank of British Columbia. It states:
The canvass was initiated as a matter of prudent foresight in late 1985 when the board of directors of the BBC concluded that BBC, like a number of other smaller Canadian banks, would have difficulty recovering from the loss of
Bank of British Columbia Business Continuation Act
confidence that followed the events then taking place in the banking system and that the time for recovery might be unacceptably long.
Therefore, we have a bank, which by all accounts was sound, well managed, put into a difficult situation where it cannot survive by the actions of the Government.
A much smaller institution in British Columbia also collapsed as a result of the Government's ill-advised and uncoordinated attempts to deal with the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. I refer to the British Columbia Teachers' Investment and Housing Cooperative. This was an organization apparently in good shape up until the collapse of the Canadian Commercial Bank when some members of the organization became anxious. There was a run on deposits which caused the organization to fold. This was a particularly difficult situation because so many of the deposits were not covered by deposit insurance. Those of us who have received very poignant letters from retired teachers who have seen their whole retirement security disappear certainly feel that the Government has a lot to answer for.
I would now like to return to the terms of the takeover of the Bank of British Columbia. This bank will be taken over by the Hongkong Bank, which is one of the world's largest. I believe it is the fifteenth largest bank in the world. It is well managed with its Canadian operations headquartered in British Columbia. Since the Bank of British Columbia has to have a merger it has undoubtedly found an acceptable partner. My criticisms are not in any way directed at the Hongkong Bank but at the Government which has again put Parliament in a situation of having to make a last minute decision in a policy vacuum.
For two years the Ministers have been dreaming and studying but not bringing forward clear decisions. The Government has not been willing to deal with the question of ownership. The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) tells us that legislation will be forthcoming within a few months. We might feel more assured by that statement if we had not heard it so often. If the recommendations of the finance committee with respect to ownership had been adopted then the Bank of British Columbia in its canvas would have had a much broader base. There would have been many other choices. Similarly, the Continental Bank would have had many other choices. However, in a policy vacuum the Government makes some type of ad hoc decision.
We will not be opposing the legislation, as I said earlier, because on the face of it this is a fair solution. Some 1,400 staff members of the Bank of British Columbia are guaranteed that their employment will continue. I believe there are about 39 branches of the bank which are expected to continue in operation. The depositors will be protected. However, the shareholders will certainly be losing something. It seems as though this solution is the lesser of the two evils for them.
There is a proposed $200 million infusion from the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, which infusion will be

November 26, 1986
Bank of British Columbia Business Continuation Act
financed by a levy on the financial institutions concerned. This, of course, means that somewhere along the line a consumer will be paying something for it. None of this would have been necessary if it were not for the Government's ill-advised actions 18 months ago and all the chaos which flowed from it.
Our leader spoke of the fact that the Bill removes from shareholders the right of approval. They have a limited right to approve the sale; but the basic right to assess the quality of the decision making is being removed from them. I am very uneasy about using Parliament for this type of measure. Again, I reluctantly recognize that it is probably the best decision that could be taken in the circumstances.
I repeat, if the Government had acted earlier with legislation we would not be so circumscribed, and nor would the Bank of British Columbia be so circumscribed in this situation. It would have had a broader range of options if it wished to have a merger or sale. If the Government had acted differently, I am convinced we would not have had such an erosion of confidence in the economy which caused the Bank of British Columbia's difficulties in the first place.
I conclude by pointing out that we on this side of the House will want fuller information from the Government with respect to this matter, more than can be had in a short debate. We will want to have committee hearings after the event. We will want an opportunity to assess the accuracy of the information provided to us today.
I can hardly say strongly enough that it is more than time for the Government to proceed with legislation. Again today the Minister of State for Finance promised us legislation "soon" on the aspects of supervision and regulation. There was proposed legislation of that type on the Order Paper before the House recessed in July. The Government chose not to proceed with it. However, the all-important and more fundamental issue of ownership has not been addressed. While the Minister of State tells us it will be addressed in the next few months, all I can say is that we have heard that before. We have been promised new legislation in two Speeches from the Throne and in innumerable statements in the House. That leaves us to ask: When, oh when?
I sincerely hope that we have seen the last of this type of ad hoc solution and that the Government will come forward with some serious attempts to define policy for financial institutions before we run out of financial institutions.

subtopic: BANK OF BRITISH COLUMBIA BUSINESS CONTINUATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a number of comments to make on this Bill. As I said in response to the Minister's statement, we come to this debate in sorrow, regret and in a great deal of puzzlement because of the lack of information upon which we have to act. I understand that there are some difficulties, because in dealing with financial institutions a great many of the discussions between Government and those institutions, of necessity, and for reasons of confidentiality, have to be carried out in secret. However, we were called in today and asked to react constructively and positively to the Government's proposal that
legislation be enacted which would, within a day or so, wipe out the provisions of the Bank Act for the protection of shareholders. We are being asked to allow this particular transfer of assets to take place, in the course of which yet another of our chartered Schedule A banks will be put under foreign ownership.
In response to the Minister I expressed my reservations and my concerns about this move. I have to say that the information which I have so far been able to find indicates that there is substantial reason to believe that there were other options available to the Government with respect to the future of the Bank of British Columbia which, for various reasons, the Government, having a major say in this, chose not to follow.
The legislation before us, Bill C-27, allows changes to the Bank Act which essentially override the provisions for the approval of shareholders of the transfer of assets from the Bank of British Columbia to the Hongkong Bank of Canada and presumably its parent company in Hong Kong. The shareholders will not be able to ruminate over this deal and come up with a decision in a month's time as it is the advice of the Director of the Bank of British Columbia, advice which has been accepted by the Department of Finance, that that would create uncertainty and that that uncertainty would be damaging to this important regional institution. Therefore, if the deal is to be consummated, it should be consummated now. The wedding night should be tomorrow night. We should not wait for another month before putting this Bill through. A period of engagement would be destabilizing for the bank.
An arbitration process is put forward in the Bill. I do not think we know how that will work because it is virtually without precedent. The shareholders have been told that the only thing they can do in a couple of weeks' time is to decide whether to accept the offer which will be in trust from the Hongkong Bank or, in the hopes of getting more, to put the matter to arbitration. They will receive some $60 million to $75 million, I am not exactly sure of the total amount, and after preferred shareholders are paid off, as we were told this morning by the Minister, shareholders will receive about 75 cents per share for common shares. Incidentally, as recently as a year or two ago, those shares sold for some $6 per share. In a few weeks' time, the shareholders are likely simply to take the money they have and run with it.
All of the evidence before us shows that in a liquidation mode, the bank is not solvent. It may be, as has been argued by Department of Finance officials, that as an operating bank it was solvent. This is a matter about which we have no information. While I have asked in the corridors for some background information about the situation, for any evaluations made available to the Department of Finance and for other kinds of information about the options, that information has not yet been forthcoming.
Perhaps I could say a word about the process. The House of Commons has moved into a new era and I think now we must
November 26, 1986

go beyond the view that the government of the day and the civil servants serving the government of the day need only provide information which supports the publicly announced decision of the Government and that no other information will be made available.
I have a number of misgivings about this particular deal. I have had a very short time to come to grips with exactly what has happened. I have had the opportunity to talk to one or two people from Vancouver and to have my research staff do some work. However, I do not know what information was availble to the Government and the only information I have is that the Government has said that this was a judgment call and we have to trust it.
The fact is that we have trusted the Government before by allowing legislation to come to third reading without unduly blocking it and we have been deceived and dismayed by the results again and again. The Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) has commented on the bail-out of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. At the Estey Commission and at hearings of the House of Commons Finance Committee with which I was involved from time to time, we have heard of a sorry story of regulation. The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) has just talked to us in rosy terms about how on the one hand the Bank of British Columbia was terminally ill and how on the other hand it would become robust and walking through the takeover by the Hongkong Bank. He has also suggested that this takeover will give British Columbia a presence in financial circles around the Pacific Rim. That suggestion, I submit, may prove to be somewhat naive. It is like saying that Canada has a presence in the world automotive market because of General Motors of Canada, a subsidiary of General Motors of the United States. Everyone knows that that is not true and that while General Motors is a productive corporation which provides much employment and has a relatively good investment record, it has next to no influence on the world-wide or American operations of its parent company in the United States.
The Bank of British Columbia, or whatever it is to be called under its new ownership, will have assets of $2 billion or $3 billion and will be part of a banking empire which stretches around the world and has particular emphasis in Australia, the United Kingdom and the Far East and assets of over $50 billion. It is an international trading bank. The Bank of British Columbia has been devoted to lending to small and mediumsized businesses. It has a network of some 39 branches in the Lower Mainland and throughout British Columbia with only one or two branches left in Alberta since the downsizing that took place a few months ago. Will the Bank of British Columbia with 3 per cent or 4 per cent of the assets of the Hongkong Bank group really have the kind of leverage it will need to influence the operations of that group or will it be in the same situation as General Motors of Canada? I could cite many other Canadian subsidiaries of American companies with far less influence, a good example of that being Goodyear Canada which has just been forced to close its plant in
Bank of British Columbia Business Continuation Act
Toronto, creating the lost of 1,500 jobs, because of corporate manoeuvring involving takeovers on Wall Street which have affected the parent company in the United States.
This is a very serious question. The Government has been looking for positive arguments to justify a measure which is difficult to justify, which at best is regrettable and which at worst may in fact be an avoidable loss of control of yet another important regional financial institution. The Government has tried to put the best face on it but I really think it exaggerates the case a bit too much according to what the Minister of State for Finance said a few moments ago.
The Minister of State also suggested that the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation was somehow acting independently in reaching a decision as to what should be done about this particular case on its injured list. I cannot believe that he can say that after looking at the composition of the Board of Directors of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. The Board of Directors consists of the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the Deputy Minister of Finance, the Superintendent of Insurance and the Inspector General of Banks. I presume that the Chairman works full time with the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation.
Does the Deputy Minister of Finance act independently when he puts on his hat as a member of the board or is he not in fact carrying out government policy? Does the Superintendent of Insurance not carry out government policy when carrying out his duties on the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Board? The same is true of the Inspector General of Banks. I am not sure if he has been replaced since Mr. Kennett offered his retirement just a few months ago.
The CDIC collects premium incomes from banks and other financial institutions but there are no representatives of the banks that provide that premium income on the board. There is no indication that the board has an independent view. It is simply a quasi autonomous government organization but nonetheless it is still a government organization.
If the CDIC was acting in place of the Department of Finance during the course of these proceedings, it is wrong for the Government to try to claim that it was somehow acting at arm's length. In fact, when I asked what had happened, I was told that the Department of Finance acted in this particular measure as a facilitator. The statement made by the Minister of State today would indicate that that was in fact the case.
It would appear that the operation of the Bank of British Columbia began to turn rather more sour sometime in the summer or fall of 1986. As a consequence, its quest for a merger or a takeover partner intensified. What we do not know and, therefore, this is one of the reasons why this is really a matter for judgment, as far as the Government is concerned, is under what circumstances that search for a merger partner took place.

Mr. Speaker, I am wondering whether or not the Government paved the way for merger discussions between the

November 26, 1986
Bank of British Columbia Business Continuation Act
National Bank of Canada, which operates mainly in the Province of Quebec, and the Bank of British Columbia.
Here are two Schedule A chartered banks which do not compete with one another since the National Bank does business in eastern Canada whereas the Bank of British Columbia deals almost exclusively within provincial boundaries.
So was there any possibility of these two banks merging or, when they did entertain such a possibility, did the National Bank know that the federal Government was quite prepared to provide $200 million one way or another to help the Bank of British Columbia get back on an even keel, to make sure it would continue its banking operations in western Canada?
In the discussions with the Vancouver City Savings Bank it was made quite clear that an injection of about $200 million was to be expected just to make sure the merger of the two banks would put both institutions on the right track.
But what I am asking, Mr. Speaker, is if the National Bank, for example, was aware of the possibility of getting $200 million in financing to make a merger possible? What about the Bank of Nova Scotia? What about the Toronto-Dominion Bank? If the Government was prepared to come in with legislation and to ask the House to legislate in order to expedite this particular deal, then was it possible that there was a trust company somewhere in western Canada, or elsewhere in Canada, that wished to enter into an arrangement with the Bank of British Columbia, and which would have done so had it been aware that the Government was prepared to bring legislation before the House of Commons?
I know that in the case of the Continental Bank when it was considering a merger with Lloyd's Bank, which is a Schedule B bank, it shied away from that particular solution on the grounds that it thought that legislation would take too long. Therefore, it chose a transfer of assets. It was able to do so with the consent of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and then of the Governor in Council in a way which effectively evaded any form of parliamentary scrutiny.
But in this particular case the Government was prepared, as apparently it was not prepared for Continental, actually to bring legislation into the House of Commons. It puts us in the Opposition into a very difficult situation. We finally have to say, "Look, you guys have chosen to take this particular course of action. We are going to have to go along with you and let you have your Bill because of the impact upon depositors and the institution if this is allowed to drag for a period of time". This is not real accountability to Parliament. This is just a debate of a couple of days. Unless overnight there is a groundswell of anger and outrage over the fact that yet another Canadian bank is being sold to foreign interests, we are in a situation where, by agreeing to allow all matters to come to a vote at 4.45 p.m. tomorrow, we have essentially
agreed to allow Parliament to be defanged and have no effective power to force the Government to back off from this particular proposal.
We do not have enough information, Mr. Speaker. All we can do is simply go along with the Government when it says, "Trust us".
I look at the list of banks which have disappeared from this country over the last couple of years, Mercantile, CCB, Northland, and now the Bank of British Columbia. There was another small one, I believe.

speechtext: The branches will be there, but it will be under another proprietorship. I am not sure if the Bank of British Columbia will keep its present name, or whether it will become the Bank of British Columbia (Hongkong). I am not sure. But, for example, the Continental Bank, which had built up a great deal of goodwill in terms of its name, is now Lloyd's Bank of Canada. It is no longer the Continental Bank. I am not sure of the arrangements. All I am saying is that this Government which is dedicated to maintaining the corporate sector and maintaining free enterprise, has presided over a tremendous disappearance of Canadian banks over the last few years. The Government has not functioned to try to keep those important institutions in the hands of Canadians. Let us be very clear about that. We are spending $200 million. It is coming out of my pocket and out of the pockets of the Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), and all of the other Members here, and every Canadian one way or the other from premiums and from taxes. That money will be paid to the Bank of Hongkong so that they in turn can turn around and buy this bank. That is exactly what is happening, of course it is coming from taxes.
