speechtext:
It is not coming from premiums. There is no money available from premiums, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of State for Finance is interrupting me, Mr. Speaker. He says it is coming from premiums. Let me read the figures. The Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation is currently in the hole, according to its last annual report, to the tune of $1.25 billion. With the increase in its premiums to three times the former rate, it will pay that off sometime in the next six or seven years, assuming that there are no further losses. After that, it can then get around to paying the $200 million which it will owe as a consequence of this particular infusion of capital into the Hongkong Bank.
Now, if I can continue-and I say this to the Minister of State for Finance, who seems to be quite worked up about this situation-in addition, over that period of time, the Canada
November 26, 1986

Deposit Insurance Corporation will have to pay interest on the money that it is currently borrowing to the Consolidated Revenue Fund. Borrowing $200 million dollars at 10 per cent per annum, and keeping it for six years until it is repaid, means that the CDIC will have to find an additional $125 million in interest for the money which is being advanced to the Hongkong Bank. The Minister nods his head. I am glad I have his agreement finally.
The point I am trying to make, Mr. Speaker, is that whether it is $200 million or $300 million, that is an awful lot of money. The CDIC, if it is going to get out from under this particular liability, will likely want to increase its premium rate yet again. The directors, all of whom are appointed by the Government and are high government officials, will turn around and will say to the Minister of State for Finance, "Look, we need to increase our premium rate again". Right now we pay through taxes or through interest on the national debt, or whatever it is, for money that is being advanced. Sooner or later we, who are customers of the banks, and we cannot help but be, and I speak for all Canadians, will have to pay for this particular reinjection of capital into the Hongkong Bank. One way or the other we are paying. Right now, I suggest the Minister is being quite specious when he states in his statement that one of his goals is to do all of this without the expenditure of public funds as part of the purchase arrangement.
I raised this question when it came to the Continental Bank. We were told that the sale of the Continental Bank was good for the shareholders because they got more dollars than if the Continental Bank had merged with a Canadian Schedule A bank. We were told it was good for the depositors because they had the backing of Lloyd's Bank which is one of the biggest and wealthiest banks in the world. We were told that it was good for the lenders because they had this source to all types of new capital. We were told that it was good for the employees because there would not be any downsizing of the bank. What we were not told was that in the meantime a substantial chunk of the financial industry in Canada was passing under foreign control. The Minister has suggested that only 1 per cent of Canadian banking assets are going under foreign control as a result of this particular deal. But it was 2.5 per cent with Lloyd's, it is 1 per cent with this particular deal. I am not sure what will come next. But that is a substantial shift in control in the matter of a couple of months. It shows no sign of coming to an end. In fact, I suspect that the Government will very shortly come to us and say that the 16 per cent limit on foreign banking assets in Canada will have to be increased, because all the Schedule B banks are getting too close to the limit, and so we will have to increase it.
1 am not sure where all that leads us. However, I can say that there has not been nearly as vigorous a drive by the Government to see whether there were Canadian solutions.

I talked with officials of the Department of Finance today. Essentially I asked them what was really going on. They said that by going with the Bank of Hongkong, by paying $200 million for Hongkong to buy our bank, we minimize the risk and we minimize uncertainty as far as the Treasury or the CDIC is concerned. The Minister cannot have it both ways. If he is trying to minimize risk to the Bank of Canada, he cannot argue at the same time that the CDIC is not the Government of Canada. Also I was told that if a Canadian solution had been pursued, there would have been greater risk to CDIC.
I find the information before us is in fact contradictory. The Bank of British Columbia was given a clean bill of health by a special inspection team of the Inspector General just 13 months ago. In its release today the Bank of British Columbia indicated that in the event of liquidation, the shareholders might come out without anything and that there might be some loss to uninsured depositors. That would suggest, according to the records of the Bank of British Columbia, that in liquidation there would be no net loss to the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation.
The Minister of State or the Government may argue that there are public policy reasons, even if that were the case, for the deal to go through in the form in which it is now proposed. Nonetheless, it suggests at the very least that there is a very substantial difference in perception between the people who know best the business of the Bank of British Columbia and the Government of Canada. The Government is saying that there will be a net loss of some $300 million or $400 million of which $200 million will have to be taken up by means of the CDIC infusion of capital. I am not sure what is the situation.
The economic situation in British Columbia has not changed that appreciably. It was pretty bad a year ago and it is pretty bad today. It is not as though there has been a sudden new and sharp downturn in the economy of British Columbia over the course of the last period of time. The Bank of B.C. says that while there might be a net loss of uninsured depositors, it is not suggesting that it will go further than that. On the other hand, the Government says that it is going an awful lot further than that.
One question must be asked-who is right? While taxpayers, either as taxpayers or as premium payers, are putting up $200 million, is it fair that the shareholders in a bank which is essentially without net worth or net assets should walk away with $60 million or $75 million? I ask that question. I cannot give an answer to it. I do not have the information from the Government. Is it in fact that it is in the form of a bribe from the CDIC so that shareholders will shut up and not make waves in terms of legal action which might impede the particular deal?

I hear the Minister of State. We are being told at the same time that the bank was finished as a going concern, if not this month, next month or the month thereafter.

They cannot have it both ways. If the bank is to be finished in a couple of months without either a merger or a takeover, the moment it became known, the bank would be finished- and the Minister knows enough about finance to know it- because banking rests so much on confidence.
Also the Bank of British Columbia indicated that no organization was identified with which a transaction on a going concern basis would have been feasible. 1 have suggested a few, but it was suggested to me that the Government of British Columbia did not want to see an eastern bank take over control of the Bank of B.C. In its view it was better to have Hongkong than eastern Canada. That is questionable. I do not necessarily want to come down on either side of that, but I suggest a better solution-better a B.C. solution than any other.
I am very disturbed that the proposed merger of the Vancouver City Savings Credit Union and the Bank of British Columbia was stymied. I want to find out why. This is one reason I trust the matter will in fact go to the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. In fact, the Minister of State has assured me that he will use his best offices-I think that was the essence of our discussion-to ensure that the matter is raised before the standing committee. Two and a half weeks ago negotiations between Vancity and the Bank of British Columbia were going well. If it took place, it would triple the size of Vancity from $1.5 billion in assets to $4 billion. It would take Vancity from 15 per cent of the British Columbia market, where it was behind the Royal Bank and the Bank of Commerce in terms of deposits, to a point where it would become the largest financial institution in British Columbia. If I may say so, the Government is putting up a red herring in suggesting that the problem was that the Bank of B.C. would become a trust company. The problem was making the necessary legislative arrangements, because it was a provincial institution, in order to ensure that the long-term merger could take place.
Frankly I have not had enough time to establish exactly what was in mind. Within a very short period of time it was intended that the Bank of British Columbia would become a kind of co-operative bank as a consequence of the merger with Vancity. The trust company solution would ensure that the Bank of B.C. could continue to serve its customers and depositors over the period of time in which that took place. As we are seeing today, when there is a political will and when there is co-operation from the opposition Parties, it is possible to put new arrangements in place very quickly. That is one of the attributes of the parliamentary system.
The problem was not between Vancity and the Bank of B.C., according to the information I have. It was the fact that the Government of British Columbia backed away from suggestions it become involved in order to ensure that there was a B.C. based regional bank. That was Premier Vander Zalm who made a number of bold promises during the course of the election campaign. When it came down to putting some money
where his mouth was, in the form of debentures which would carry interest and would have been repaid, he backed away.
When it came to the role of the federal Government, it was simply asked to have CDIC take over a portion of the debt of the Bank of B.C. It was soft debt or questionable debt. Since the shareholders would begin by absorbing their losses, it was very unlikely that it would have come up to $200 million. The net cost to the federal Government would have been the same or less as this particular solution. The net benefit to B.C. would have been an institution which remained a British Columbia institution.
Since 1982 there has been no increase in loans from the big five chartered banks in British Columbia. In other words, they have not been doing the job of putting money raised in deposits back into the province. They have increased their deposits in B.C. by $10 billion since 1982, but they are not putting money back into the economy of British Columbia. While we talk with reason about the need for a regional banking institution in British Columbia or in western Canada, there is also a responsibility on the part of chartered banks to do their job and not to suck dry financial assets from western Canada in order to lend them abroad or to bring them into Ontario or central Canada. That has been the complaint of British Columbians for a long time. I say to my hon. friends from British Columbia that I speak as a native of B.C. who was born in that province in 1937 and as someone who retains a certain attachment to the province even though I was moved by my parents at a somewhat early age.

I will see what my constituents have to say about that.
Another matter I should like to raise is that obviously the Bank of British Columbia could not make up that shortfall in deposits on its own. There is an over-all problem in terms of banking policy toward British Columbia in which the Government since 1984 could have and should have become involved but did not.
We do not know if there is a job guarantee from the Bank of Hongkong. I note there is no reference to it in its statement. We do not know what kind of bank or business plan it has. The Government says that it does not know what is the business plan. In other words, they are buying on the reputation of the Bank of Hongkong, not on specific commitments to Canada. The Hongkong Bank is an international trading bank. I suspect one of the reasons the Government has bought this solution is that it believes that it will somehow encourage the desire to make Vancouver an international financial centre.
November 26, 1986

I will have some words to say at some other time about the proposed tax exemption being discussed. Most people who are experts in the banking system say that whatever the political rights or wrongs of the proposal, it is unlikely to bring banking business to Canada that would not otherwise have come here. Will an international trading bank with business on four or five continents want to continue to provide loans of $200,000 to $2 million to motel operators, hardware store operators, outfitters, tourist operators and that kind of thing in the interior of British Columbia? Is that possible or will the Hongkong Bank in its new role as the owner of the Bank of British Columbia decide that that is not the strategic direction the Bank should follow?
I was looking for a list of the bank's branches in the interior of British Columbia, but unfortunately I do not have it. But from Hong Kong to Kamloops, from Hong Kong to Lillooet, from Hong Kong to Port Alberni, is there a real fusion of interest that will allow branches in those areas to continue to be in operation, or will we see a further pruning of the Bank of British Columbia in order to turn it into an international trading bank? If that is the case, Mr. Speaker, I suggest we might have been a lot better off having kept this institution under Canadian control.
What about the question of the head office? If the head office of the Bank of British Columbia (Hongkong) is going to be in Vancouver, does that mean decisions will be made there, or will the real decisions be made at North American corporate headquarters in New York or in world headquarters which, I presume, are in the Far East? I do not know. I think that is a very relevant question. It is certainly clear that the Government has not used any leverage at all in seeking to get answers on those questions from the Hongkong Bank. Nothing I say is to denigrate the stability, the size or the reputation of the Hongkong Bank. It is one of the largest banks in the world. I go back to the example of Continental and Lloyds. If every time we have a Canadian financial institution in trouble we allow it to be taken over by a stronger institution, we will wind up with no financial institutions in Canada in Canadians hands. They will all be bought up by banks or other financial institutions abroad which happen to be bigger than most of our Canadian financial institutions.
What arrangements has the Government made for additional branching? We do not know. That is a question I have to which it is not possible at this moment to have an answer. I would ask the Minister of State and his officials to provide as much information as is possible between now and tomorrow prior to our going into committee on this Bill. I would like to raise a number of questions with him and his officials at that time.
It does seem to me, however, in looking-

-it seems to me as a Member of the Opposition who has examined this Bill that the only sound and valid reason to
Bank of British Columbia Business Continuation Act
adopt this measure is simply the argument that, if after studying the Bill the House of Commons were to endorse the Government's option to allow the Bank of British Columbia to be sold to this foreign institution, the Hongkong Bank, the only justification would quite simply be that a long period of uncertainty might compromise the survival and profitability of the Bank of British Columbia under its new owner, the Bank of Hongkong.
Of course, if the Government uses its majority to provide for the financing with this Bill, or if the two banks, with the approval of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Governor in Council were able to transfer assets without permission from the House of Commons, it would be our responsibility as Members of the Opposition to accept the situation. This does not mean we agree with the Government's decision, but we must accept its right to make that decision.
However, there are all sorts of precedents indicating that many mistakes have been made on the initiative of the Inspector General of Banks, and that may have been the case last October, when the Inspector General judged the Bank of British Columbia to be in good shape. We are now hearing statements to the effect that the Bank is not in good shape.
There are many indications that this Government, because it has delayed introducing a new policy on financial institutions, has allowed our financial institutions to lose a considerable amount of funds and credibility.
We have seen how much this has cost taxpayers through taxes and the premiums paid to the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. It cost us nearly one billion dollars after the collapse of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northlands Bank. Now we are spending, either directly or indirectly, a total of $200 million that will go to a foreign bank, which in turn is going to pay $60 million to the shareholders of the Bank of British Columbia.
I find it very difficult to support this measure. We are being asked to accept the Government's judgement that this is the best solution available, despite the fact that the Government has done practically nothing in the way of looking for and supporting a truly Canadian solution, such as a merger with the National Bank, with one of the chartered banks in Eastern Canada or the merger that was almost achieved with the Vancouver City Savings Credit Union, an institution with assets of $1.5 billion and which, I believe, was quite capable, with the support of this Government and the provincial Government of British Columbia, of becoming the real owner.
The Canadian or regional option was ignored in favour of a foreign option.

We have lost sight of the possibility of regional solutions. Instead the Government has chosen to have solutions which involve alienating once again the control of a prominent and important regional and Canadian financial institution by putting it into foreign hands.

subtopic: BANK OF BRITISH COLUMBIA BUSINESS CONTINUATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, problems with our financial institutions is not a subject matter in which one should revel or celebrate. I know that the Government has been working on this matter for a considerable period of time and has monitored the situation. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Flockin) should be complimented on coming forward with a solution that minimizes the loss to Canadian taxpayers.
Mr. Speaker, the Act which is Bill C-27 which is before the House is a Bill to facilitate the continuation of the business of the Bank of British Columbia. 1 think those words in themselves are of great significance to all of us that are British Columbians. 1 know one of the dreams of W.A.C. Bennett, a man who governed our province as Premier from 1952 into the 1970s, was to have a regional bank to deal with the concerns and needs of British Columbians. Today, as we prepare the legislation that will maintain or continue the operation of the Bank of British Columbia, I think it is a positive step.
With regard to the legislation, the Government has been guided by four basic considerations, Mr. Speaker, in this transaction. Firstly, to ensure the long-term financial viability and continuation of the institution. Secondly, to provide to the fullest extent possible for the needs of its depositors, other creditors, borrowers and shareholders. Thirdly, to serve the needs of the westernmost part of Canada and to do so without the expenditure of federal public funds as part of the purchase arrangement. In addition to that, it secures the jobs of bank employees at the 39 bank branches. Job security has to be a significant factor. When we look at the plight of the employees and the high level of unemployment in British Columbia, the unacceptable level that the federal Government is making every effort to reduce at the present time, this particular aspect of the legislation definitely has to be taken into consideration.
Members of the NDP spoke about their dislike of foreign ownership. Philosophically and ideologically they oppose any foreign ownership in Canada. They compare the situation of this bank with the Goodyear closure in Toronto. There is really no comparison. Obviously, if you are philosophically opposed to something, there is no way you can accept it. Any critical remarks they make in this situation have to be seen in that light. The NDP Members also made reference to General Motors in this context. That company is a good, responsible corporate citizen. It may be foreign-owned but it is a part of Canada. This is a huge country with too small of a population and that is why we have to attract foreign investment, but under our terms of reference.
I would now like to speak about the Hongkong Bank of Canada. It is a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank Corporation. It began operations as a Canadian chartered bank in Canada in July, 1981. As of October, 1986, its assets exceeded $735 million. It offers the entire range of banking services such as term and operating credits,
trade financing, deposit services, foreign exchange, remittances, documentary credits, personal banking, private banking, and assistance with business activities in the Pacific Rim. We have to address the importance of the Pacific Rim countries as trading partners for British Columbia, and I will deal with that a little later. The bank has its head office in Vancouver with offices in Toronto, Montreal, Edmonton, Calgary, Saskatoon, Winnipeg, Halifax and Victoria. The Board of Directors has five Canadians and two non-resident representatives of the shareholders. The Chairman is Angus R. Petrie, and the President and Chief Executive Officer is Eugene Nesmith of Vancouver. That is an indication of the bank's intention to do business in Canada utilizing Canadians and making the entire operation a Canadian operation.
We also have to look at the fact that it is a world-wide bank. The Hongkong Bank group, headquartered in Hong Kong, has consolidated assets exceeding $108 billion as of June 30, 1986. It has 1,200 offices in 55 countries with more than 46,000 employees. That is an indication of the financial depth and strength of this institution. Members opposite have referred to the fact it is a foreign-owned bank with branches in Australia and New Zealand. That fact will be of assistance to us. It will give us a common interest with the Pacific Rim countries and countries like New Zealand and Australia. We on the West Coast have to establish a more viable trade relationship with these countries. We cannot be as dependent as we have been on our trading partner immediately to the south. Members of the Hongkong Bank include a multitude of banks, including the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation and the Marine Midland Bank, just to name two. This is another indication of the bank's tie-in with the world banking community. Other companies in this group are involved in commercial and merchant banking, investment management and financing, as well as leasing and insurance services. There are more than 400 branches in Hong Kong and an extensive Asian branch network in one of the world's most rapidly developing areas. It has more than a century of experience in financing international trade. These are the things that Canada and British Columbia need.
As the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) pointed out, I do not think anyone in Canada would settle for anything less than total Canadian ownership if it were possible. That would be Utopia. Unfortunately, that is not the way it is in the real world. The credentials of the Hongkong Bank of Canada are impeccable and it will bring financial stability and security to the banking community, especially the Bank of British Columbia.
In dealing with some of the problems in western Canada we have to ask why these banks failed. That question is going through the minds of a lot of Canadians, including my constituents in Mission-Port Moody. People like Alistair Brown are really concerned, wondering just what has happened to cause these bank failures. I guess the first question you have to ask is whether it is a matter of regulation. What kind of regulation? Should the regulations be changed? Should they become more stringent? Should we have done it more quickly? Should the previous Government have taken a
November 26, 1986

stronger role in changing the regulatory environment which governs these institutions? Or is this simply an indication of the economic plight of western Canada? That is something western Canadians have tried to point out to eastern Canadians time after time. Or is it possibly the policies of the federal Government in the late 1970s and early 1980s which led to high interest rates and runaway inflation? These are some of the questions we have to ask as we enter this debate on the problems the banks are facing.
As a small businessman in the housing construction business in the late 1970s and early 1980s, 1 can tell you unequivocally that high interest rates and runaway inflation, as well as Ottawa's monetary policies, are at least partly responsible for the dilemma we are facing today. Eastern Canadians have to understand what is really taking place in western Canada today. Let us consider the commodities industries, such as the grain industry. There are massive subsidies by the European Common Market, and the United States Government is massively subsidizing grain in retaliation. This is devastating the economy of the grain farmers in western Canada.
We can look at the mining industry. It is suffering one of its worst slumps in our history, and there is no indication of an improved market. Our coal industry is barely holding on as a result of the reduced orders from our major customers in the world. The forest industry in British Columbia is plagued by a strike that has resulted in some $20 billion in lost income. This is compounded by the uncertainty brought on by the countervail action of the U.S. lumber industry under the International Trade Commission.
The really devastating impact has been the price drop in the world oil market. The federal Government and eastern Canadians, especially those in central Canada, must understand that all of these factors combined have led to a severe economic dilemma in western Canada. We are not asking for hand-outs, just for consideration. The uniqueness of our industries and of our sources of income means that we must have banks with their headquarters located in our regions so they can understand our uniqueness and the needs of our various industries and agricultural sectors.
There are Members who oppose the free trade initiative. 1 mention free trade because the free trade initiative and the other requirements 1 have mentioned are a prerequisite in establishing a viable and strong economy in western Canada. We cannot terminate this very positive initiative of the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) because in order to remain viable and enhance our economic position, a free trade agreement with the United States is absolutely necessary.
If we do not establish such a free trade initiative, there will be further countervail actions like that taken by the U.S. lumber producers. We will become islands, without a secure access to at least 250 million people. We will become nontraders as opposed to the aggressive traders that we are today.

Dealing with regional disparity must be a priority. That is why the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) and the Minister of Finance have seen fit to take the action they have in regard to the banking dilemma facing western Canada.
The Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) referred to bail-outs of banks. The banks were not bailed out, the depositors were assisted in that situation in western Canada. We must address the western economy as a whole and the British Columbia economy in this case. Let us consider what the Government has done to assist western Canada and assist British Columbia in removing any economic uncertainty and providing banks, businesses and British Columbians with an opportunity to prosper.
I want to review some of the events that I believe were devastating and caused the collapse of banks in certain cases and required the consolidation of others. I believe the National Energy Program was one of the most devastating programs for any region of Canada, and it was one of the major contributing factors to the dilemma that these banks in western Canada faced.
Since you have indicated that I only have two minutes left, Mr. Speaker, let me say in conclusion that Parliament was requested by the private sector to take this initiative. We were asked to assist in facilitating this transaction.
The management of the Bank of British Columbia advised the Government that this transaction is necessary for its survival. The Government agrees with that assessment. The Bank of British Columbia announced today that its Board of Directors believes that it is essential for the bank to enter into a transaction if liquidation is to be avoided. The board further believes that no other transaction can be identified that would be as beneficial as the proposed transaction with the Hongkong Bank of Canada.
Smooth transition is another aspect that had to be taken into consideration. Parliament was asked to expedite this private sector transaction in order to ensure the smoothest possible transition, in the best interest of all concerned.
Shareholders' interest had to be taken into consideration. The legislation recognizes the interests of shareholders. It provides for a shareholders' meeting, with 14 days notice, to approve the consideration received for the sale of the bank's assets, or if the shareholders so choose, an independent assessor will be appointed to evaluate the worth of their shares immediately prior to the time of sale. This evaluation would be binding.
The transaction does not appreciably increase the level of foreign participation in the banking sector. The level is raised slightly, to 12 per cent of the assets of the entire system, which is well below the permissible 16 per cent.
The transaction has the support of British Columbians. The Member for Ottawa Centre questioned the role played by the Premier of the province. The Premier of the province was elected by the majority of British Columbians, and we are

proud to have a Premier with such a strong majority in British Columbia. I know it was a moral victory for the NDP, but it was a true victory for Mr. Vander Zalm.

Mr. Speaker, for the second time in about fifteen months here we are in the House debating the banking situation, the possibility of a bank going under, or situations such as we are experiencing today. I have no intention of going over the debates and arguments we had when we examined the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank failures because obviously we would have to rehash the past and repeat many of the arguments which focused on the Government's incompetence when it comes to the administration of its own financial institutions, particularly with respect to the western banks, the Northland Bank and the CCB, and now the Bank of British Columbia.
Mr. Speaker, this time I do not understand anything. I do not understand anything because, for openers, the Government wants us to act quickly without giving us full details and, secondly, those we do have are contradictory. If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment on some of the information given to the public at large by these financial institutions, more specifically on the information made available about the Bank of British Columbia. In the document provided by the Financial Post information service which reports-this is not an analysis-which reports a number of facts, we read this among other things, and if I may, Mr. Speaker, I will quote the report on the Bank of British Columbia.

November 26, 1986

An inspection of the bank's loan portfolio was completed in October, 1985 by a special team of inspectors acting under the jurisdiction of the Inspector General of Banks. The review concluded that the bank's loan portfolio was "sound".

Mr. Speaker, the Inspector General of Banks conducted a special investigation of the Bank of British Columbia and reached the conclusion that its loan portfolio was sound.
He goes on to say that in the course of a year, the percentage of losses on loans had dropped and that percentagewise, non-performing loans were below the average for the banking sector. That was in October 1985. If we look at how the Bank evolved since then, and I have been looking at quarterly and annual results, we see the following: after nine months, on July 31, 1986, the Bank's net profit was $6,653,000, compared with $5,696,000 for the first nine months of the previous financial year, an increase of nearly one million dollars, and this information supported the conclusions of an investigation conducted by the Inspector General of Banks, which indicated that the Bank's loan portfolio was sound.
Mr. Speaker, we are told that the bank is in great difficulty. It was always my understanding that the problem at the Bank of British Columbia was not the loan portfolio but the deposits, and that what happened to the Canadian Commercial Bank in Alberta and the Northlands Bank had created a climate of uncertainty, leading depositors to withdraw their money, and that the loan portfolio was sound. Like many other Members of this House, I had every reason to believe the report of the Inspector General of Banks who had conducted a special investigation in October 1985. Today, we are told it is not a matter of depositor confidence but of the value of the Bank's assets. The Minister goes on to say that this Government, through the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, will be giving $200 million to the Bank of Hongkong which will be used to purchase all or almost all of the assets of the Bank of British Columbia for $63 million. They are going to put $200 million into the assets of the Bank of British Columbia, as a branch of the Bank of Hongkong, without receiving in return any shares or ownership in the new bank that will have been created. They are going to give it to the Bank of Hongkong, and-

-the Hongkong Bank of Canada will buy the Bank of British Columbia or place in a trust fund for shareholders some $63 million. That is the deal that we have in front of us.
I cannot understand why the Canadian Government will take $200 million from the pockets of Canadians in one way or another, through insurance premiums or otherwise, to place it into the equity of the Hongkong Bank, British Columbia Division, while at the same time allowing the shareholders $63 million. There is something wrong with that. If the assets of the bank are sound, as was suggested in the report of the Inspector General of Banks in October of 1985, then I see no reason why the Government would put $200 million into this deal. The Minister cannot have it both ways. Is it that the
report of the Inspector General of Banks was wrong, or that since October of 1985 the situation has deteriorated substantially?
We do not know exactly what happened because we do not have the facts. What the Bank of British Columbia told us in its statement dated November 26, 1986, is that liquidation is not a reasonable alternative as realized asset values, in the view of the Bank of British Columbia's board, would be affected to the point that it would be questionable whether any amount would be available for the shareholders of the BBC and there might well be a loss to uninsured depositors.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, this is a very serious matter, because according to the Board of Directors of the Bank of British Columbia, liquidation would, to all intents and purposes, mean the loss of all assets held by common and preferred shareholders, of subordinate debentures and of cumulated surpluses, if any. Furthermore, uninsured depositors would be put in a loss situation.
Mr. Speaker, if that is the case, I ask the Government: Why take $63 million in taxpayers' money, because the taxpayers are in fact paying for the insurance premiums that are paid out of the banks' surpluses, and basically, Canadian depositors, whether they have their deposits in banks or credit unions all contribute towards guaranteeing deposits of up to $60,000-why take $63 million to protect shareholders who knew perfectly well that by taking shares in a bank they were taking a chance and that they were not protected in any way?
Mr. Speaker, I think it is incredible the Government should be proposing this kind of solution to the problem.
In this case I am saying to the Government that, if the assessment made in the Bank of British Columbia report sent to the shareholders accurately depicts the existing situation, and if chances are that liquidating the bank's assets would entail similar losses, this means, and already I can hear the tacit argument of the Minister, namely that as a going concern it may have some value. Fair enough. I agree, it has some value. But, as I see it, only if the same shareholders are involved.
If, as a Government, we were to decide to maintain a regional bank and use Canadian taxpayers' money, not as taxpayers but as depositors in financial institutions on which, as depositors, they pay premiums through the financial institutions which take their money, then 1 say: Why not add the $200 million to the assets of the Bank of British Columbia shareholders and give BBC shares to the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation? Why not take the risk, if we are going to hand the money over to the Hongkong Bank, why not take the risk with the present shareholders of the Bank of British Columbia and keep the bank going as a regional institution which can operate normally? Because, I will be told, it was a matter of long-term credibility.

November 26, 1986

Until now, Mr. Speaker-

Well, if it is not enough it is because somebody somewhere is not doing his job. What 1 cannot understand is that, although it is enough for the Hongkong Bank, it is not enough for Canadian taxpayers. As a matter of fact, just what is the position of Hongkong Bank management? They say: We put up $63 million, we get $200 million to boot, so we will go ahead and buy a network of 39 branches with 200,000 depositors and a ready-made clientele. Try and develop a network of 39 bank branches and build up a certain reputation and attract 200,000 to 300,000 depositors. Try and do this within a financial institution and see if it doesn't cost at least $63 million. It's a good deal for them. It certainly is. It would be a good deal for just about any foreign bank that does not have a network and that wants to buy one. I wonder, however, why we are taking taxpayers' money to do this. And if we do, and that is what the Minister is suggesting- Yes I realize they will assume all the Bank's liabilities, but they are getting $200 million to help them do that, $200 million that will go into their equity. Imagine! The Bank of Hongkong doesn't have to do much to have the lowest ratio between assets and equity of any bank in the Canadian system.
They already have $200 million which isn't costing them a cent, and there are assets worth $2.8 billion. They're starting practically with a ratio of one to ten. All they have to do is put in a few million more and they will have the lowest equity to asset ratio there is in our banking system and our financial institutions here in Canada, except perhaps for the other bank that was taken over, which of course had practically no deposits and was very highly leveraged, as they say. But I don't think that is a very relevant example.
Mr. Speaker, the fact remains that they have taken $200 million in taxpayers' money-I don't think we have to quibble about this being taxpayers' or other people's money-it all belongs to Canadians, because the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation belongs to Canadians. They are taking $200 million and giving it to the Bank of Hongkong, which then turns around and buys almost all the assets for the sum of the $63 million, and also assumes responsibility for the Bank's liabilities, as the Minister said. I should hope so.
I submit, with respect, that taking the money of Canadians to sell one of our financial institutions to foreign interests, and Em not questioning the competence of the Bank of Hongkong, on the contrary, 1 think they are very astute businessmen to have managed this kind of deal, and if they manage the bank as well as they managed the deal with the Government, 1 think the new bank's depositors can rest easy.
However, the fact remains that if the Government is at all concerned about good management of public funds, and if we want to help British Columbia have a bank that is regional and managed by their own people, we do not take $200 million and
Bank of British Columbia Business Continuation Act
give them away to foreign interests. We take the $200 million and make a deal with the present shareholders. The Minister says it might cost more than that. And I say to him: He must have ... Well, I suppose the Office of the Inspector General is somewhat confused these days, but somewhere in this Government there must be somebody and there are experts elsewhere as well who can determine exactly what is involved.
If these $200 million . . . Mr. Speaker, as a Member and on behalf of Canadian taxpayers, I would much rather support a $225 million payment and end up with Bank of British Columbia shares held by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation than hand over $200 million and never again see the colour of my money. Why, with 200 or 225, if I am wrong the Minister will correct me later. We will have a question period, but right now he is disturbing my concentration. Perhaps that is precisely what he wants to do.
If the solution I am advocating were to be accepted, the shareholders of the Bank of British Columbia would continue to be shareholders of the Bank of British Columbia. The Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation would become a BBC shareholder. Let no one talk to me about nationalization, we are not dealing with theology here, this is a practical matter because we are going to pay out $200 million. If we were to form a partnership, the Canadian people with the Deposit Insurance Corporation and the present shareholders, I am sure that with such an asset to equity ratio we would be able to restore confidence and maintain a regional bank under the management of British Columbia residents and for the benefit of British Columbia residents. What we are doing now ... It is true that the bank will stay in British Columbia, it is true that it will employ local people, but any decision concerning a wholly-owned branch whose head office is in Hongkong will be made by management in Hongkong.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would have many other questions to raise, but I have only 20 minutes. I would like to say something about the bank staff.
Mr. Speaker, the Hongkong Bank will acquire most of the assets.
We are told-and I have yet to receive confirmation of this-that the 39 branches will be kept open. We do not know yet. There are 1,400 employees. In the case of the merger, of the take-over of the Continental Bank's assets by Lloyds Bank of Britain, we were told all the employees would be maintained in their jobs.
This time we have no such assurance. Firstly, we have no assurance that tomorrow morning the new owners who were given a $200 million handout to buy a business for $63 million will guarantee those employees'jobs.
Secondly, according to the Board of Directors, discussions are still going on with the Inspector of Insurance and Superannuation Plans for $10 million to be withdrawn to the benefit of the Bank of British Columbia's present shareholders, and if

November 26, 1986
Bank of British Columbia Business Continuation Act
such a request is guaranteed or accepted over the coming months, that money could be redistributed to the shareholders. Not only is the Hongkong Bank given $200 million to buy the Bank of British Columbia, and shareholders given $63 million, part of their assets, but $10 million may be taken out of the employees' superannuation fund to increase the price the shareholders will be getting for their shares.
Mr. Speaker, this is written in black and white on the document I have before me, which was published by the Bank's Board of Directors, and from which I quote:
During the second quarter of the fiscal year 1986, the Superintendent of Insurance approved the withdrawal of surplus contributions from the pension fund of BBC based on an independent actuarial report. After the Bank's year end the Superintendent of Insurance, in view of subsequent jurisprudence, revoked his permission to withdraw these surplus funds, but has left it open for BBC to re-apply to withdraw the surplus in accordance with new guidelines. This may result in BBC having to reverse $20.4 million of pre-tax income during 1986.
In connection with the sale to Hongkong Bank of Canada, it is proposed that the pension plan account balances of all BBC employees will be transferred to an equivalent pension plan with the Hongkong Bank of Canada. BBC will re-apply to the Superintendent of Insurance for permission to withdraw the surplus funds remaining in its pension plan. If the application is successful, this surplus would accrue to the benefit of the shareholders of BBC.

If, Mr. Speaker, in addition to giving $200 million to a bank which, according to its own board of directors, is not just insolvant but would be nibbling at uninsured deposits, if in addition to handing out those $200 million, we allow them to use the superannuation fund to increase the amounts the shareholders would be getting, I am at a loss to understand. What I am saying is, we will have to pass the Bill because we have no choice, and because the Government insists that if we do not pass it the whole system will collapse. Mr. Speaker, I must tell you it is with the utmost reluctance that I am going to support the Bill. It is only because the Government is pointing a gun at our heads that we must take its word for it. I had really promised myself after March 25, 1985, when we were asked to approve the package to solve the problem of the Canadian Commercial Bank that I would never again take the word of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) about a banking matter. Yet, once more, we have to give our approval because we are asked urgently to pass legislation to maintain a financial institution in Western Canada, to protect jobs and to keep an institution under foreign control in business. I must say that it makes no sense to ask responsible Members of Parliament to approve such a measure in only 24 hours.

Now that the price is low, not due to Canadian producers but due to a decision taken by the cartel, the elevator should have gone up and helped western producers. However, government Members destroyed the elevator, so they

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry, but I should like to participate in the debate. I thought I would have at least 10 minutes in which to put a few comments on record.
As a western Canadian I am deeply concerned about what happened today. We have seen a western Canadian financial institution going down like ten pins. I agree with some of the comments of Hon. Members opposite which point to the fact that the source of the problem is in the past. However, for the Government to believe that the only reason was the National Energy Program of the Liberal Party is to delude itself. It is a case of bad management on the part of the previous Government and as far as this Government is concerned.
We have been promised reforms. We have been promised legislation dealing with financial institutions for almost two years. Members of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs spent last summer travelling the length and breadth of the country to hear submissions. We have been promised legislation, but the Government has not brought in any legislation. I do not think the Government knows where to go.
It is not surprising from a Government which believes in the free market economy that it would let the free market sort it out. However, this generally means as far as Conservatives are concerned that if there are profits to be made, they should not be touched. On the other hand, they believe that if they are in
difficulty, public funds should be used to bail them out. We have seen the Government bail out several major financial institutions. Now it is doing it again.
The Government is helping the shareholders of the Bank of British Columbia and it is helping the Bank of Hongkong. I sat here listening to members of the Conservative Party from British Columbia who said: "But we are saving a regional institution". I do not understand. Again it is Orwellian thinking. How can the Bank of Hongkong be a regional institution?
I am also greatly concerned about the types of guarantees we will have. Will the head office remain in British Columbia? What will happen to the 1,400 employees? What will happen to the branches throughout the interior of British Columbia? Is the Bank of Hongkong interested in keeping open a branch in the interior? Is it interested in keeping open branches in local communities and in servicing local communities? Is the Bank of Hongkong only interested in some of the major branches in Victoria and Vancouver?
Unfortunately we are again in a position where we have a gun to our heads. We should be discussing the details of the matter in committee before being asked to vote.
What efforts did the Government make to find Canadian buyers? I have read in the press that Vancity was very interested in taking over the Bank of British Columbia. I want to know what type of negotiations occurred. Why was it not possible for Vancity, a Canadian institution owned by the people of British Columbia, to take over the Bank of British Columbia? Many very important questions need to be asked. Unfortunately we are being asked to vote on the Bill without hearing the answers.
